title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 3 (23/02/2018)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 23 FEBRUARY 2018
Subject: The Claimant challenged one of the Arbitrators (appointed by the Respondent)
pursuant to Articles 12 and 13 of the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules 2010.
Outcome: Upheld
Seat: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
Governing Law of Brazilian law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to the Arbitrator’s: (i) previous employment with the
Respondent; (ii) pending lawsuit against the Respondent; (iii) participation in
three ongoing academic projects with one of the Respondent’s counsel; (iv)
alleged attendance and speaking engagements at event(s) allegedly organised
by the Respondent; and (v) failure to disclose some of these circumstances.
The Claimant argued that these circumstances raised justifiable doubts as to
the Arbitrator’s independence and impartiality.
The LCIA Court upheld the challenge.
By referring to “justifiable doubts”, the UNCITRAL Rules impose an objective
approach which requires considering the point of view of a reasonable third
party. For the challenge to succeed, the Claimant’s – necessarily subjective –
concerns about the Arbitrator’s impartiality and independence have to be
objectively reasonable.
The Arbitrator’s previous employment with the Respondent for more than 20
years, ending more than 15 years ago, creates justifiable doubts about the
Arbitrator’s independence. Even if the Arbitrator may now be reasonably
assumed to be financially independent from the Respondent, there may be
other types of dependence, such as dependence for referrals of work, for
recommendations for contacts and contracts with third parties, or for
information of relevance to the Arbitrator’s work.
The Arbitrator’s employment with the Respondent for more than 20 years,
also creates justifiable doubts about the Arbitrator’s impartiality, because of
the length of the period of employment (more than 50% of the Arbitrator’s
professional life) and the fact that the Arbitrator’s career continued within the
same industry and field of practice.
Under Brazilian arbitration law, the Arbitrator’s pending lawsuit against the
Respondent also prevents the Arbitrator from acting in a case involving the
Respondent.

The Arbitrator’s three ongoing joint research projects with the Respondent’s
current in-house counsel (who is also a member of the Respondent’s legal
team in the arbitration), raise justifiable concerns regarding the Arbitrator’s
impartiality and independence.
The Arbitrator’s participation in a congress allegedly organised by the
Respondent is insufficient to support a challenge. Assuming that the
Respondent was the organiser, it cannot be determined whether the
Arbitrator’s participation in the congress is the mere result of the academic
standing of the Arbitrator or existing affinity between the Arbitrator and the
former employer or the in-house counsel.
The Arbitrator’s failure to disclose the pending lawsuit against the Respondent
alongside the Arbitrator’s cooperation with the Respondent’s in-house
counsel in a Moot Court team is not in itself a ground for challenge but renders
more justifiable the Claimant’s doubts arising from the other grounds.
Decision 3 - 2

LCIA COURT OF INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION
Arbitration N° […]
[…]
CLAIMANT
v
[…]
RESPONDENT
Decision on Challenge of an Arbitrator
___________________________________________________________________________
I. PROCEDURE
1. This arbitration arises out of a dispute between [the Parties], resulting from [the] Respondent’s alleges
breaches during the performance of the […] Agreement (“Agreement”) entered into by [the Claimant]
and [the Respondent] […] for the Claimant’s services […] in certain areas in Brazil, which were granted
to the Respondent as a concession from [a] Brazilian [authority].
2. The arbitration clause contained in the Agreement provides for arbitration in accordance with the
Arbitration Rules of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (the “UNCITRAL
Rules”), in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Each Party was to select an arbitrator in accordance with the
UNCITRAL Rules and the arbitrators so nominated were then to agree within thirty (30) days on a third
arbitrator to serve as Chairman. The clause further provides that the proceedings shall be
administered by the London Court of International Arbitration (“LCIA”) and that if the nominated co-
arbitrators are unable to agree on a Chairman, then the President of the LCIA shall appoint the
Chairman.
3. According to the arbitration clause, the language of the arbitration is English. However, in para. 30 of
its Notice of Arbitration of 20 June 2017, the Claimant suggested that, since both parties are Brazilian,
Decision 3 - 3

the contractual performance took place in Brazil and all the communications between the parties were
in Portuguese, the language should be changed to Portuguese (without, however, any need to present
translations of documents originally drafted in English). The Respondent agreed to this suggestion.
The documents transmitted to the undersigned for purposes of deciding the challenge were either in
Portuguese or official translations into English of Portuguese documents. The Parties have been made
aware of - and have not objected to – the fact that a non-Portuguese speaker would be deciding the
challenge on the basis of English translations of the relevant documents.
4. The LCIA, in accordance with its usual practice, asked the Parties’ appointees to sign statements of
independence. The Respondent’s original appointee stepped down following comments provided by
the Claimant in relation to his disclosure. The LCIA Court thereafter allowed the Respondent to re-
appoint an arbitrator within 15 days.
5. On 28 September 2017, the Respondent appointed [A] as a co-arbitrator […]. It filed simultaneously
the curriculum vitae, as well as the Declaration of Independence and Impartiality and Consent to
Nomination of [A]. The latter document (dated 26 September 2017) contained a disclosure as follows:
“I have worked as a lawyer for [the Respondent for more than 20 years]. From then on, for [more than
fifteen] years, I worked as a lawyer, legal advisor, or counselor of several legal entities of different
companies and entities, besides [my role in an academic institution]. … I have never acted as a lawyer,
reviewer or arbitrator of [the Respondent] after [the year I left]. On several occasions I have prepared
opinions of interest to [an association]. I declare to be independent and impartial to act as arbitrator,
as determined by art. 13 § 6 of Law No.9307 of 1996 (as amended […])”.
6. On 13 October 2017, the Claimant challenged this appointment pursuant to Articles 12 and 13.1 of
the UNCITRAL Rules, and requested that the challenge be decided by […] the London Court of
International Arbitration (“LCIA”), the appointing authority chosen by the parties in the arbitration
clause. The Claimant also requested with reference to article 14. 2 of the UNCITRAL Rules that, after
the dismissal of the Respondent’s co-arbitrator, the […] LCIA appoint a co-arbitrator in Respondent’s
place.
7. On 30 October 2017, the Respondent objected to the challenge rejecting, in their entirety, the
Claimant’s allegations in support of the challenge.
8. On the same date, [A] (hereafter also “the Arbitrator”) informed the LCIA that she did not wish to
withdraw and that “there are no circumstances that give rise to justifiable doubts as to her impartiality
and independence to act as co-arbitrator in this arbitration”.
9. On 13 November 2017, the Claimant confirmed its intention to pursue the challenge, filed some
additional documents in support of its challenge and requested the […] LCIA Court to decide the
challenge and appoint another arbitrator on behalf of the Respondent.
Decision 3 - 4

10. On 29 November 2017, the Respondent submitted a further reply to the challenge and confirmed its
request that [A] be confirmed as arbitrator and that, in the alternative, should the challenge be
accepted, it be entitled to appoint another arbitrator.
11. The LCIA Court first attempted to appoint for the challenge decision [a relevant person] fluent in
Portuguese, but the candidate declined the appointment due to a conflict of interest. The Parties have
thereafter agreed that the LCIA Court would select [someone else], who would read the challenge
submissions in English and issue a decision in English. The Parties were subsequently made aware that
the LCIA Court had asked [someone] to determine the challenge, who had previously agreed to decide
the challenge but withdrew following objection by one of the Parties. Thus, on 30 January 2018, the
undersigned […] was informed that the LCIA Court had selected her to determine the challenge.
12. On 7 February 2018, the Parties were informed of the appointment and received a copy of the signed
statement of independence and consent to appointment. No objections were formulated.
13. On 9 February 2018, the Claimant, having been informed of a change of law firm by [A], requested
that she provide clarification to certain questions concerning the link between her new law firm and
another company in the [industry] sector [relevant to the dispute], […]. The Claimant clarified that it
did not intend to modify the basis of its challenge submission with such correspondence, and that the
undersigned should be exempted from examining such correspondence.
II. CLAIMANT’S GROUNDS FOR CHALLENGE
14. The Claimant bases its challenge on article 13 § 6 of the Brazilian Arbitration Act and on article 12 of
the UNCITRAL Rules, relying on four circumstances which the Claimant alleges to represent justifiable
doubts as to the impartiality and independence of [A]:
1. She worked as an in-house counsel for the Respondent for [more than 20 years], from […] to […].
The Claimant acknowledges that the Arbitrator disclosed this fact voluntarily in her statement of
independence and added that during the […] years since then, she “never acted as a lawyer, reviewer
or arbitrator of [the Respondent] after [leaving employment with the Respondent]”. Nonetheless, the
Claimant considers that her relationship with the Respondent goes far beyond that of a former
employee, and is a very close one which continued to be nurtured during the following years, given
her dedication to Respondent’s market segment.
2. A […] court case filed by [A], as Claimant, against the Respondent.
The Claimant notes that the Arbitrator had not disclosed being involved as plaintiff in a law suit against
the Respondent […]. The Claimant invokes article 14 of Brazilian Arbitration Act No. 9,307/96 providing
that “persons who have, with the parties or with the litigation submitted to them, one of the
Decision 3 - 5

relationships that characterize cases of inability to sit or recusal of judges are prevented from acting
as arbitrators, as the same duties and responsibilities as provided in the Code of Civil Procedure, are
incumbent to them, where applicable”. A judge cannot sit when he has a suit against a party (art. 144,
item IX of the Code of Civil Procedure (the “CPC/15”) and when a party is a debtor of the judge (art.
145, item III of the CPC/15). [A]’s law suit against the Respondent renders both articles applicable to
her.
3.[A]’s participation in three ongoing academic projects with one of the Respondent’s counsel.
Her CV reveals that she is cooperating with [B], who is one of the Respondent’s in-house legal counsel,
acting as one of its attorneys in the present case, in the following projects:
- [Project C];
-[Project D];
-The […] University team which is competing in the […]Moot […] is supervised by the Arbitrator and
[…] by [B], as the Claimant discovered on the internet;
According to the Claimant, these projects prove the Arbitrator’s academic, intellectual and personal
proximity to the Respondent’s attorney.
4.[A]’s attendance and speaking engagements at events organized by the Respondent, “the most
recent being in […]”.
The Claimant points out that the Arbitrator did not give any explanation on this connection to the
Respondent, but instead stated that she had no links with the Respondent since [leaving employment
with the Respondent].
15. In its confirmation of the pursuit of the challenge of 13 November 2017, the Claimant denies that the
Respondent’s and the Arbitrator’s comments of 30 October 2017 can dispel the existence of justifiable
doubts as to the Arbitrator’s independence and impartiality:
- the mere existence of the [law]suit against [A] constitutes an objective situation of conflict of
interest: the arbitrator has a credit against the Respondent;
- impartiality and independence are the first requirements for an arbitrator and the fact that the
Respondent’s first appointee had no qualifications in the field of exploration and production, prove
that the specialized knowledge is not indispensable;
- the Abitrator’s multiple professional experiences cannot erase the link she had with the Respondent
for more than 20 years;
Decision 3 - 6

- the […] law suit is addressed not only against [E], but also against the Respondent, which has at [A]’s
request been held jointly and severally held with [E] for the Arbitrator’s claim;
- the Claimant never agreed to the application of the IBA Guidelines on conflicts of interest and in any
event articles 4.4.1 and 4.5.3 do not apply to the academic links between [A] and [B] and the fact that
there is not one, but three joint projects (of which one, the moot court team, was not even disclosed),
confirms the affinity and continuous contact between the arbitrator and the representative of the
opposing party;
- the fact that [A] has “multiple academic works and hundreds of participations in events, as in many
or almost all of them there were companies and law firms as co-sponsors, in Brazil and abroad”, does
not minimize the fact that she lectures in events organized by Respondent as a result of the good
relationship and the link between them,
III. THE RESPONDENT’S RESPONSE
16. In its response of 30 October 2017, the Respondent reacted to the first three of the four above
challenge grounds as follows:
1.The academic relationship of the Arbitrator with the attorney of the Respondent is covered by the
“green list of the Guidelines of the Brazilian Institute of Arbitration – IBA – concerning Conflicts of
Interest in international arbitration” as a result of which there is no duty to disclose (i) a relationship
between an arbitrator and a counsel of one of the parties by virtue of affiliation in the same class
entity or social organization (art. 4.4.1) and (ii) joint work as joint experts or in another professional
capacity (art. 4.5.3)1. It denies that there is any personal proximity in a research project that
encompasses several [academics] from the [University] and states that an academic relationship does
not impact on an arbitrator’s independence and impartiality and that it is inevitable that the
professionals working in the still expanding field of arbitration in Brazil are in contact with each other.
2.The employment relationship dates more than 15 years ago and culminated in […] litigation, so if
someone has to fear partiality, it should rather be the Respondent. The Respondent points out that,
as it had in the past a [significant involvement in] the exploration and production of [the relevant
product] in Brazil, it is hard to find an expert in this field who had no connection with the Respondent.
Referring to the Arbitrator’s CV, the Respondent points out that the Arbitrator has continued her
successful career in the [relevant industry] sector during almost 20 years totally independent from the
Respondent and has even developed activities in competing companies and against the Respondent.
By appointing her, the Respondent only intended to have one of the most respected professionals
currently in the [relevant] industry with extensive expertise in the field, join the tribunal.
1 The numbering and the text, presumably translated from Portuguese, appears to correspond to numbering of
the 2004 IBA Guidelines.
Decision 3 - 7

3.The Respondent acknowledges the incompatibility for judges as laid down in the CPC/15, but
considers that the required specialized competencies distinguish this case.
17. The Respondent repeated these arguments in its objection of 29 November 2017, and addressed also
the fourth ground, concerning the Arbitrator’s alleged participation in events organized by the
Respondent. The Respondent refers to para. 28 of the Claimant’s statement2 about one such
conference [….] and notes that this congress was organized by [an association], a legal entity distinct
from [the Respondent].
IV. THE ARBITRATOR’S COMMENTS
18. [A]’s comments of 30 October 2017 on the challenge first clarify her legal background and
qualifications:
• she has been working in the [relevant] industry for [many years];
• she has been [teaching] law for [many years]; and
• […].
19. She then addresses the alleged grounds:
1.In connection with her in-house counsel work for the Respondent, she repeats the statement in her
declaration of independence: she undertook counsel work for the Respondent [for more than 20
years], after which she has not acted for the Respondent as either counsel or legal advisor, nor has
she been nominated (or appointed) as by the Respondent.
2.The court case against the Respondent, where the Arbitrator appears as claimant, is a […] matter
[…], […] against [E], […], which does not affect her impartiality and independence to act as co-arbitrator
in this arbitration; she sought to obtain complementary pension payments for her in-house counsel
work […], which are guaranteed by law, and such claim is not material to the Respondent.
3.As regards the academic projects and speaking engagements, the Arbitrator points out that although
most academic events are sponsored by companies and law firms, the economic beneficiary is always
the event/conference and not the individual, speaker or attendee.
20. The Arbitrator confirms that there have been no circumstances known to her – in her professional
and academic careers – likely to give rise to any justified doubts as to her impartiality and
independence.
2 The reference apparently should be para. 25 of the Claimant’s Notice of Challenge of 13 October 2017 which
referred to the reference in the arbitrator’s CV to [a conference]. The undersigned could not find this reference
in the 51 pages of the – non searchable – document.
Decision 3 - 8

V. ADMISSIBILITY
21. According to article 13 of the UNCITRAL Rules, the notice of challenge has to be sent within 15 days
after the challenger has been notified of the appointment of the Arbitrator, or within 15 days after
the circumstances mentioned in articles 11 and 12 became known to that party.
22. The Respondent informed on 28 September 2017 the LCIA and the Claimant of the appointment of [A]
as its arbitrator (see acknowledgement of the Claimant in para. 1 of its challenge that it received the
hard copy of the Respondent’s letter on 28 September 2017). The challenge is dated 13 October 2017.
The undersigned is therefore satisfied that the challenge was submitted within the 15 day time limit
under article 13 and is admissible.
VI. ANALYSIS OF THE CHALLENGE GROUNDS
23. The challenge is based on article 13. 6 of the Brazilian Arbitration Act which requires that “the
arbitrator shall act with impartiality, independence, competence, diligence, and judgment” and on
article 12.1 of the UNCITRAL Rules providing that:
Any arbitrator may be challenged if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the
arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
24. Neither Respondent nor the Arbitrator contested the legal and regulatory frameworks indicated by
Claimant as applicable to the analysis of the existence of justifiable doubts as to the Arbitrator’s
independence and impartiality. The Parties agree that there need not be evidence of actual partiality
or dependence, but the Claimant points out that the appearance of these deficiencies suffices,
whereas the Respondent emphasizes that mere doubt is not enough. The concrete question to be
resolved is whether the doubts are justifiable because of one or more of the four circumstances shown
by the Claimant.
25. By referring to “justifiable doubts”, the UNCITRAL Rules impose an objective approach which requires
taking into account the point of view of a reasonable third party. For the challenge to succeed, the
Claimant’s – necessarily subjective - concerns about the Arbitrator’s impartiality and independence
have to be objectively reasonable. All relevant facts and circumstances have to be taken into account
when ascertaining whether the Claimant’s apprehension or fear of bias is reasonable.
26. The four “circumstances” invoked by the Claimant are but various aspects of links which exist between
the Arbitrator and the Respondent. They are interrelated, in that the oldest circumstance, the past
employment of the Arbitrator by the Respondent, has lasted a long period of time and that the other
circumstances can be seen as a natural consequence of that employment.
Decision 3 - 9

1. Past employment by the Respondent
[paras. 27-29 redacted]3
30. The preceding paragraphs are only an excerpt from the 51 page long CV which details thereafter the
many activities in terms of conferences, courses, publications and legal services of the Arbitrator, also
after her departure from the Respondent and until today. The CV is impressive and the Respondent
ánd the Claimant agree that the Arbitrator is highly competent and specialized in the subject matter
of the arbitration for which she was appointed.
31. There is no doubt that the [more than 20] year-long employment by the Respondent has been, in
combination with the Arbitrator’s personal capacities, the feeding ground for her present
specialization in [the disputed area of] law and her familiarity with the [relevant] industry. The
question whether the Claimant’s concerns about the Arbitrator’s present independence and
impartiality from this employer are justified, has two aspects: the independence and the impartiality.
32. As regards the independence, it may be reasonably assumed that [A] is today financially independent
from the Respondent. She has left the Respondent [more than 15] years ago and has – apparently
successfully and intensively - continued her activities, both academic and professional. Her declaration
that after [leaving employment with the Respondent], she has never acted as a lawyer, reviewer or
arbitrator for the Respondent may be understood to mean that she has not received any payment
from that company since she left. Her reputation as a specialist and expert in [the disputed area of]
law is by now fully her own and has reportedly led her to render legal services to competitors of [the
Respondent] – […]. The CV mentions indeed services to e.g. [a competitor]. Financial independence
does not mean that there may not be other types of dependence, however, such as, e.g., dependence
for referrals of work, for recommendations for contacts and contracts with third parties, or for
information of relevance for her work. Doubts about the Arbitrator’s independence are in the given
circumstances justifiable.
33. Impartiality is yet another issue. This is a less objective criterion than dependence. Moreover, the state
of mind in terms of impartiality is difficult to ascertain when an arbitrator has not yet become active
on a case, as his/her subjective disposition towards the parties cannot be scrutinized against the
background of his/her conduct in the arbitration. So here the question how a reasonable third person
would consider the circumstances, becomes even more pertinent. The long period of employment
([more than 20 years] as acknowledged by the Arbitrator herself, notwithstanding the small
unexplained gaps mentioned above) is a crucial factor which has to be considered in the light of (i) the
length of the period since the termination of the employment and (ii) the continued emphasis on [the
disputed area of] law in the Arbitrator’s further career. The period of employment by the Respondent
is even today still several years longer than the time which lapsed since she left the Respondent, and
in fact exceeds more than 50% of the Arbitrator’s professional life. Even assuming an eventual total
career of 45 years, it will still represent almost half of that career. This is a very long period, even for
3 […]
Decision 3 - 10

someone who started that career in a period when job-hopping was not as frequent as today. Since
moreover, the Arbitrator, notwithstanding the further expansion of her horizons, has remained
faithful to the [relevant industry] business, the departure from Respondent was not so much a rupture
or a split, but a continuation of a road taken. The Respondent is at the origin, and was during [more
than 20 years] the core, of the Arbitrator’s activities in and for the [relevant] industry. During all those
years, the Respondent has trained and formed the Arbitrator, allowed, supported and possibly even
encouraged her parallel educational and academic initiatives and activities and introduced her to
other players in the [relevant] business. It is only normal that the mutual loyalty, which is sufficiently
proven by the [more than 20 years] of employment relationship, is enhanced by a proportional quality
of the relationship. Such long period necessarily creates a considerable degree of familiarity and
identification with the employer, both the institution and the individual colleagues. Even if the
relationship has been terminated [more than 15] years ago, it cannot but have created a bond which,
at least in the eyes of any third person makes an impartial approach very unlikely.
34. The fact that the Arbitrator is presently engaged in a law suit with the Respondent is insufficient to
make the concerns, based on the long employment relationship, less justifiable. As discussed
hereafter, the law suit concerns a claim about pension rights against the Respondent and [E] and the
file does not contain any indication that this claim is based on, or has as a consequence, any animosity
between the Arbitrator and the Respondent, which could neutralize the positive effects and mutual
benefits of their long relationship, which in the eyes of an outsider may raise justified doubts about
independence and impartiality.
2. Lawsuit between the Arbitrator and the Respondent
35. Neither the Respondent, nor the Arbitrator deny that article 14 of Brazilian Arbitration Act No.
9,307/96 (quoted in para. 15.2 above), in combination with articles 144, item IX and 145, item III of
the CPC/15, apply in this instance, but they minimize the relevance of the violation. The Respondent,
which did not even address the issue in its Response of 30 October 2017, states in its 29 November
2017 Response that “although the hypotheses of impediment and suspicion of the judge
contemplated in the Civil Procedure Code are applicable to the arbitrators, the interpreter must apply
them in light of the elements of the concrete case” and emphasizes parties’ right to appoint arbitrators
they find competent and that “to close such right would mean annihilating the defendant’s
contribution to the formation of the [arbitral tribunal]” (p.9-10). The Arbitrator specified that the case
is in its enforcement stage and that this pension claim does not affect her impartiality and
independence and is irrelevant to the Respondent.
36. The undersigned notes that neither the expertise of the Arbitrator, nor the fact that the Respondent
is not the sole respondent in the law suit (but is sued as a joint and several debtor together with [E]),
nor the fact that the law suit is in the enforcement stage, nor the fact (which has not been made
explicit, but which may be understood from both the Arbitrator’s and the Respondent’s comments on
this issue), change anything to what appears to be an objective infringement of the above mentioned
rules of Brazilian law. As neither the Respondent nor the Arbitrator have provided evidence that these
Decision 3 - 11

rules must not be applied strictly or are not applicable in international arbitration, the undersigned
cannot but conclude that pursuant to article 14 of Brazilian Arbitration Act No. 9,307/96 in
combination with articles 144, item IX and 145, item III of the CPC/15, the Arbitrator is prevented to
act as an arbitrator in a case involving a party which she has sued and which is (considered as) her
debtor.
3. Ongoing academic projects with one of the Respondent’s counsel
37. The undersigned notes that the two research projects mentioned in the Arbitrator’s CV which the
Respondent has pointed out involve one of the in-house counsel representing the Respondent in this
arbitration, have been started at least 3 or 4 years ago and will continue for an unspecified period of
time. The cooperation between the Arbitrator […] and [B] [for] the [University] team in this year’s […]
Moot Court competition does not figure on the CV of the Arbitrator (and was not otherwise disclosed
by the Arbitrator) but was discovered by the Claimant on the internet. The CV shows yet another joint
field of activity of the Arbitrator and [B]: they participate regularly together in “conclusion papers
boards”, both for the master degrees and for the master qualifications at [the University]. As regards
the cooperation in the [University] team preparing for and participating in the [..] Moot Court
competition, it is noted that this is an annual event and that the cooperation of the Arbitrator and [B]
in this field is likely to have lasted already [for some] years, as [B]’s website4 shows that he was already
a coach in [a previous year].
38. It is only normal that the intense academic activity of the Arbitrator necessarily entails multiple
contacts and joint projects with academic colleagues (many of whom are also mentioned, besides [B],
in her CV). However, the multitude and variety of academic contacts of the Arbitrator with numerous
former students, PhD scholars, assistants and colleagues, in the view of the undersigned, cannot
outweigh the Claimant’s concerns about her contacts in three ongoing joint projects with one of them,
when that colleague is, besides an [academic] at the [University]5, also an in-house counsel of the
Respondent and one of the nine attorneys representing the Respondent in its arbitration with the
Claimant6. That the Arbitrator herself has also been an in-house counsel of the Respondent and thus
shares not only an academic but also a professional background with her young colleague, is not likely
to alleviate the concerns about the collegial familiarity, proximity and affinity which, even if not
personal, are understandably disturbing for the trust which the Claimant should have in the
Arbitrator’s impartiality and independence.
4. Attendance and speaking engagements at events organized by the Respondent
4 […]
5 ibidem
6 see the list of attorneys – in which he figures as second - in the Respondent’s responses to the challenge and
the email address mentioned there: […]
Decision 3 - 12

39. The undersigned could not determine which is the source of the Claimant’s reference to find the
mention of “[a conference]”.7
40. Even assuming that the Arbitrator participated or even spoke at this congress, the mention as such is
insufficient to prove that the congress was organized by [the Respondent] as alleged by the Claimant;
which allegation is, moreover contradicted by the Respondent. Furthermore, the Arbitrator’s reaction,
that sponsorship of conferences by companies benefits the event/conference and not the individual,
speaker or attendee, is correct. However, this only confirms the financial independence of the
speaker, in casu the Arbitrator. Whether her role in the congress is the mere result of her academic
standing or of her proximity and affinity with her former employer or its in-house counsel – assuming
that the Respondent was the organizer – cannot be determined.
5. Failure to disclose
41. The Arbitrator’s failure to disclose the pending lawsuit against the Respondent and her cooperation
with [B] in the […] Moot Court team, is not in itself a ground for challenge. However, it makes it difficult
to adopt a less strict approach of the application of article 14 of Brazilian Arbitration Act No. 9,307/96
and renders the doubts of the Claimant following from the four substantive grounds even more
justifiable.
VII. REPLACEMENT OF THE ARBITRATOR
42. The Claimant alleges that the Respondent did not adequately discharge its onus of appointing an
arbitrator because it was aware of the facts which gave rise to the challenge and because there was a
similar flaw in the appointment of the first arbitrator. It considers the Respondent’s appointments as
a “delaying move” which justify that it be deprived of its right to choose its own arbitrator and that
the appointing authority appoint the substitute arbitrator pursuant to article 14.2 of the UNCITRAL
Rules.
43. The undersigned cannot agree with the Claimant’s allegations of intentional and repeated obstruction
as suggested in the statement that “it is the second time that the Respondent intends to nominate as
co-arbitrator a professional who knowingly does not meet the basic requirements for the exercise of
such role”. While it is not clear whether the “knowingly” is used in relation to the Respondent or in
relation to the nominated arbitrators, there is no evidence of conscious misinformation either by the
Respondent or by the Arbitrator. The challenge grounds were not easy to decide to the extent that
the subjective concerns of the challenger have to be “objectivized” in order to determine whether
these concerns are justifiable. Certainly for persons, such as the Arbitrator, who consider themselves
independent and impartial and may indeed be so, it is not always easy to realize how or why other
persons might have concerns in this connection. This makes the disclosure duty a difficult one.
Moreover, for people with a long and active career, the number of possible disclosable facts may be
7 See also footnote 2 above.
Decision 3 - 13

huge. Unintentional negligence may therefore not be excluded and, even a CV which could fill in
omissions in the disclosure, may have gaps. To the extent the “knowingly” referred to the Respondent,
the undersigned finds that the Respondent’s explanation about its concern to have an arbitrator on
the tribunal who was an expert in [the disputed area of] law deserves credit (even if the expertise
cannot outweigh the impartiality concern). The Respondent, as the Arbitrator, clearly believed that
the [more than 20] year-long employment of the Arbitrator was outweighed by the time elapsed since
then and the Arbitrator’s clear disclosure in this respect confirms that there was no intention to hide
anything. That the undersigned considers the doubts of the Claimant justifiable does not mean that
the Respondent or its arbitrator acted improperly.
44. Consequently, there is no reason why the Respondent should not be given the opportunity to
nominate a substitute arbitrator. That the search for a suitable candidate may be more difficult since
the parties agreed to deviate from the arbitration clause by agreeing that Portuguese would be the

VIII. DECISION
